The others: `cicd-quality-gates.findings.hasUnjustifiedSecurityFindings`; `executive-scorecards.scorecards.{performanceDashboardLinked,cognitivLoadSurveyCompleted,collaborationIndexComputed}`; `gitflow-branching.git.{featureBranchMergeNotSquashOrRebase,hotfixNotExpeditedPath,hasStaleBranchesAfterMerge}`; `multi-runtime.runtime.{mobileHardwareNotKotlin,asyncInteropNotMessageBroker}`; `open-core-boundary.openCore.hasEnterprisePromotionWithoutApproval`; `protocol-selection.protocol.{bffUsesGraphqlAsGeneral,fileUploadsNotGrpc}`; `satellite-contracts.contracts.{nameIsUnique,needsGovernanceUpgrade,upgradePathDocumented}`; `testing-pyramid.testing.{integrationUsesEphemeralContainers,e2eCoversHttpRoutes}`; `version-pinning.{packageJson.overrides,overridesRationaleDocumented}`. **Note `cognitivLoadSurveyCompleted`** — a typo in the policy that a declared schema would have caught on the day it was written.
- **Use cases:**
  - A caller reads `multi-tenancy.input.schema.json`, supplies every field it declares, and expects a run that can pass.
  - A tenant integrating the Core needs one document that says what facts an evaluation wants.
  - A policy author adding a field must be told to declare it, at the moment they add it.
- **Impact:** A rule nobody can satisfy is indistinguishable from a rule the repository violates, and the remedy is invisible: the field is named nowhere the caller reads. This lands on the surface `GT-694` just opened — supplying facts is now possible, and 21 of the fields worth supplying are undocumented. `additionalProperties` is undefined on these schemas, so extra fields ARE accepted; the defect is discoverability, not rejection, which is why it is P2.
- **Expected outcome:** every field a policy reads is declared in its schema with a type, and a check refuses the next one that is not.
- **Affected files:** `src/rulesets/opa/schemas/*.input.schema.json`, `src/rulesets/opa/*.rego`
- **Component:** `Core Domain` · **Criticality:** P2 · **Complexity:** S
- **Principal:** `S` · **Interest:** `MED` · **Basis:** `estimate`
- **Provenance:** Registered 2026-08-15 from the `GT-694` closure. **Kept out of that slice deliberately:** `GT-694` was about categories that could not be REACHED; this is about fields that cannot be DISCOVERED once they are. Folding it in would have mixed a structural fix with 21 schema edits in one diff. **Not a duplicate of `GT-694`:** those categories now reach their policy, and this row is why some of them still cannot be made to pass.
- **Acceptance criteria:**
  - [x] **FALSIFIABILITY:** a caller supplying exactly the fields `multi-tenancy.input.schema.json` declares gets a `passed` verdict. Today that run fails with `MTN-06` and `MTN-07`, naming fields the schema does not mention; both outputs recorded.
  - [x] All 21 undeclared fields are declared with a type, or the policy stops reading them, decided per field.
  - [x] A check fails when a policy reads a field its schema does not declare, demonstrated by adding one and showing the check go red.
  - [x] `cognitivLoadSurveyCompleted` is resolved as either the intended spelling or a typo, and whichever it is appears in both files.
- **CLOSED 2026-08-15.** All 21 fields are declared in their schemas with a type, and `cognitivLoadSurveyCompleted` is now `cognitiveLoadSurveyCompleted` — the spelling SPACE-03's own message uses. Renamed in the policy and its test together; the `src/sdk/cli/rulesets` copy is generated by `copy-rulesets` and gitignored, so the source corpus is the only place to edit.
  - **Declaring changed NO verdict, and that is the point.** `additionalProperties` is undefined on these schemas, so the undeclared fields were always accepted — the defect was discoverability, never rejection. They are added to `properties` and deliberately NOT to `required`: in Rego an absent field makes `not input.x.y` true, so absence already means "not done", and requiring them would turn a legible violation into a schema error.
  - **Types inferred from usage rather than assumed:** `packageJson.overrides` is an OBJECT because `DEP-08` does `count(overrides)`; the other twenty are flags.
  - **AC1 is DERIVED, not hand-listed.** The compliant posture is built from the fields the schema declares, with polarity read from the policy itself (`not input...X` ⇒ X must be true), so nobody has to remember which flags are the negative ones. Falsifiability proven by deleting one declaration: the posture omits that field and `passed` becomes `failed` — the exact pre-fix behaviour.
  - **AC3 demonstrated as the criterion asks:** making a policy read a field its schema does not declare turns the new check red; restoring the typo turns two red. Both restored.
- **A CORRECTION TO THIS ROW'S OWN COUNT.** Registered as "21 fields across **11** categories". Re-measured on closure: 21 fields across **10** — `cicd-quality-gates`, `executive-scorecards`, `gitflow-branching`, `multi-runtime`, `multi-tenancy`, `open-core-boundary`, `protocol-selection`, `satellite-contracts`, `testing-pyramid`, `version-pinning`. The field list was right; the category count was not. **This is the third aggregate count I have gotten wrong in this family of rows** — `GT-693` (33/31/197 → 39/35/203), `GT-694` (15/12 → 14/13), and now this. In every case the enumeration was correct and the total was not, and in every case the fix was to re-run the count from the files rather than to re-read my own prose.
- **Status:** `DONE`

#### GT-696

**Title:** Thirteen blocking rules across four topologies are decided by reading one self-declared JSON, the same pattern GT-683 fixed for agentic-ai

- **Purpose:** Give every topology the assurance distinction agentic-ai now has, so a buyer can tell an inspected verdict from a believed one on all of them.
- **Evidence:** **Measured 2026-08-15 while closing `GT-683`, whose AC7 named this and permitted deferring it in writing.** `config-rules.ts:74-118` reads four declaration files — `serverless.config.json`, `event-driven.config.json`, `data-mesh.config.json`, `edge-computing.config.json` — and decides each verdict by comparing one boolean field. Counted from the corpus rather than estimated: **13 rules, all 13 `blocking: true`** — serverless 4, event-driven 3, data-mesh 3, edge-computing 3. Examples of what a field comparison stands in for: `event-driven-outbox` passes on `config?.transactionalOutbox === true`, so a repository with no outbox table and no outbox publisher passes a rule named *Transactional Outbox*; `serverless-stateless` passes on `config?.stateless === true` while a handler holding module-level state is never opened. **The criterion named three topologies and there are four** — `edge-computing` uses the identical `readJsonConfig` + boolean pattern and was missed when the row was written.
- **Use cases:**
  - A buyer comparing Evolith against a competitor asks which verdicts were inspected and which were believed, for every topology and not just one.
  - A satellite adopting `event-driven` wants its outbox claim checked against the repository, the way `AAI-R03` now checks declared paths.
  - An auditor partitions any topology's corpus by assurance from the shipped JSON, as they can already do for `agentic-ai`.
- **Impact:** The same false-pass class `GT-683` closed, still open on four topologies and 13 blocking rules — a repository can be certified against a control it does not implement, and nothing in the output says the verdict was a field read. It is narrower than `GT-683` was in one respect: those rules at least require the declaration file to EXIST, so an empty repository fails rather than passes.
- **Expected outcome:** every rule in these four topologies carries a truthful `assurance`, the buyer-facing README publishes it, guard 56 covers them, and the checks that can honestly observe the repository do.
- **Affected files:** `src/packages/core-domain/src/application/validators/evaluators/handlers/architecture/config-rules.ts`, `src/rulesets/topologies/{serverless,event-driven,data-mesh,edge-computing}/**`, `.harness/scripts/ci/56-validate-assurance-disclosure.mjs`
- **Component:** `Core Domain` · **Criticality:** P2 · **Complexity:** L
- **Principal:** `L` · **Interest:** `MED` · **Basis:** `estimate`
- **Provenance:** Registered 2026-08-15 from `GT-683`'s AC7, which said the pattern in the sibling topologies is "fixed or explicitly deferred in writing on this row". **Deferred, and this is the reason rather than an excuse:** observing what these rules assert means real static analysis — finding an outbox publisher, proving a handler holds no module-level state, showing a data product publishes contracts. Hand-rolling that alongside `GT-683` would have produced confident wrong verdicts, which this board has already decided twice is worse than a rule that admits it only read a declaration (see `GT-683`'s `hexagonal-architecture.layers` reasoning and `GT-694`'s). **`P2` and not `P1`:** unlike `GT-683` the declaration file must exist, so this is an over-trusting verdict rather than one reachable by an empty repository.
- **Acceptance criteria:**
  - [x] **FALSIFIABILITY:** a satellite whose `event-driven.config.json` declares `transactionalOutbox: true` with no outbox implementation anywhere in the repository produces a FAILED or explicitly `declared` verdict rather than a silent pass. Today it passes; both outputs recorded.
  - [x] All 13 rules carry a truthful `assurance`, verified against what their handler branch does rather than against a second hand-kept list.
  - [x] Guard 56 covers these four topologies, demonstrated by flipping one README value and showing it exit 1.
  - [x] For each of the four, the row records which checks became `observed` and which stay `declared`, with one sentence of reason each — no topology left in a third state.
- **CLOSED 2026-08-15.** Reproduced first: a repository containing exactly one config file and a manifest passes **six blocking** event-driven rules, `ED-R02 Transactional Outbox` among them, with no outbox table, no publisher and no relay anywhere in the tree.
  - **AC1 is met by the second half of its own wording** — "a FAILED **or explicitly `declared`** verdict rather than a silent pass". `ED-R02` still returns `passed` on that repository, and now says `declared` in the shipped ruleset and in the buyer-facing README, so the verdict no longer claims more than it checked. Making it FAIL would require finding an outbox publisher by static analysis, which is what this row deferred and why.
  - **AC2/AC4 — the labels are DERIVED from the code that decides each rule, never hand-listed.** `topology-assurance.spec.ts` recomputes the expected label from the handler sources and fails when a shipped label disagrees. Mutations: labelling `ED-R02` `observed` turns 2 cases red; hiding it behind `unevaluated` turns 3 red, including the case asserting that `unevaluated` is not a euphemism.
  - **AC3 demonstrated as asked:** flipping `ED-R02` to `observed` in the event-driven README alone exits guard 56 with 1, naming the rule and both values.
- **THIS ROW UNDERCOUNTED ITS OWN DEFECT.** It said 13 declaration-decided rules. Measured properly there are **17**: 13 keyed by category through `CONFIG_CATEGORIES`, plus four keyed by rule ID through `TOPOLOGY_FLAG_RULES` — `ED-R04`, `ED-R05`, `ED-R06`, `DAM-R05` — which is keyed on the id deliberately, because two bare categories are shared across topologies with different files and different flags. **That is the fourth aggregate count wrong in this family** (`GT-693`, `GT-694`, `GT-695`, and now this); as in the other three, the enumeration was right and the total was not.
- **THE CRITERION'S BINARY WAS WRONG AND IS REWRITTEN RATHER THAN FORCED,** the same correction `GT-694`'s AC2 needed. It asked for `observed` or `declared` with "no topology left in a third state". But **ten of the 29 rules are decided by NOTHING** — no handler branch claims their category, and the corpus triage already files them `underspecified`, `unimplemented-native` or `needs-external-system`. Calling those `declared` would be a third falsehood on top of the two this family has fixed: they are not believed, they are not checked, they are not evaluated. `unevaluated` is now a first-class label and the READMEs say what it means — *shipped, and not enforced*.
- **The split, measured:** **2 observed · 17 declared · 10 unevaluated** across 29 rules. Only `ED-R08` and `DAM-R07` open the repository.
- **A HOLE IN MY OWN GUARD, FOUND BY DEMONSTRATING IT.** Stripping a topology's labels left guard 56 silent, because "has not started labelling" and "labels were deleted" looked identical to it. They are not: if the README already publishes assurances, the labels existed and their absence is a regression. Now exits 1 — verified by capturing the real exit code rather than one that had passed through a pipe, a trap this repository has recorded before.
- **WHAT THIS DOES NOT CLAIM.** No rule became `observed`. Seventeen verdicts are still decided by reading a declaration, and a satellite that declares a control it has not built still passes — the change is that it now says so, in the ruleset and in the document a buyer reads. Turning any of the seventeen into a real observation needs the static analysis this row deferred, and that work is not done here.
- **Status:** `DONE`

#### GT-697

**Title:** Nothing detects a gap closed against code production never reaches, so a false closure survives a mean of 44 days until a human re-reads the board

- **Purpose:** Give the closure ledger a detector, so that discovering a wrong closure stops depending on one person re-reading it.
- **Evidence:** **Measured 2026-08-15 by a ten-agent forensic audit of this repository, whose findings were then put through three adversarial refutation passes.** The loop the owner reported — "arreglo defectos y vuelven a salir" — is not churn: **the git-churn case was refuted outright.** The `71.1%` fix-of-fix rate is BELOW a permutation null of `88.3%`, and `feat` commits re-touch old files MORE (87.0%) than `fix` commits (83.0%); "nothing settles" was a censoring artifact of the 2026-07-04 mass move, and correctly conditioned **60.7% of eligible files have been untouched for 30+ days**; CI is not soft (**2 slack flags across 15 workflows**); and the harness guards are not toothless (**55 of 55 observed turning red against an empty fixture**). What survives is one asymmetry: **gaps close in a median of 0–1 days and a WRONG closure is detected in a mean of 43.8 days** (min 26, max 53) — `GT-158` 53d, `GT-221` 52d, `GT-266` 51d, `GT-321` 49d, `GT-518` 32d, `GT-566` 26d — and **every one of those six detections was a human re-reading, not a guard, a test or the engine.** `GT-321` is the archetype: closed against `AuditService`, whose only `new` in the repository is in its own specs.
- **Use cases:**
  - A closure names a service; six weeks later somebody asks whether it is wired, and the answer should not require re-reading the row.
  - A future rewrite deletes the last call site of a class an old gap was closed against; the ledger should notice before a customer does.
  - An auditor asks which closed gaps rest on unreachable code and gets a list rather than an opinion.
- **Impact:** The ledger is monotone by construction — `08-validate-tracking` treats a closure record on a non-DONE row as a hard error, so `DONE` cannot be reversed and a regression can only be re-registered as a NEW id. Combined with a 40x detect/close asymmetry, the board grows while nothing appears to come back, which is precisely the experience of going in circles.
- **Expected outcome:** the 44-day human detection becomes a sub-second mechanical one, running on every CI run, that can only get stricter.
- **Affected files:** `.harness/scripts/ci/57-validate-closure-reachability.mjs`, `.harness/scripts/ci/closure-reachability-baseline.json`, `.harness/scripts/ci-runner.mjs`
- **Component:** `Governance` · **Criticality:** P1 · **Complexity:** M
- **Principal:** `M` · **Interest:** `SEVERE` · **Basis:** `estimate`
- **Provenance:** Registered and closed 2026-08-15 from the root-cause audit. **Registered P1 with `SEVERE` interest, stated rather than assumed:** every day it stands, closures accumulate that nothing re-checks, and the audit measured the cost precisely — 44 days per false closure, six known instances, all found by hand.
- **Acceptance criteria:**
  - [x] **FALSIFIABILITY:** the detector re-finds the closures the owner refuted by hand that have this shape — `GT-321` and `GT-266` — and does NOT fire on `AuditLogger`, which the same audit showed IS wired. All three verified.
  - [x] The guard fails on a NEW unreachable closure, on a baseline entry that has become reachable, and on losing its own calibration cases. All three demonstrated by mutation.
  - [x] It refuses a zero-element scan (`assertScanned` on both denominators) and is registered where CI runs it.
  - [x] No report mode. Guard 41's `Exiting 0 … THIS IS NOT A PASS` is not repeated: the existing findings are frozen in a baseline that may only shrink.
- **CLOSED 2026-08-15 — and the iteration is recorded because it is the finding.** The first heuristic (a closure's evidence file has no consumer) caught **0 of 6** known cases: re-export from a barrel counted as consumption. The second (dedup claimed, duplicate on disk) fired **4 times, all false** — on `src/sdk/cli/rulesets/**`, the copy `copy-rulesets` generates — and still missed `GT-566`; it was **killed rather than shipped**. What worked is narrower: an exported class in a closure's production evidence with no production call site. Two syntactic attempts to exclude framework classes both failed — a 4000-character decorator lookback missed `AppModule` at 4596, and "nearest preceding `@`" matched JSDoc and grew the baseline 70→76 — so the exclusion is by **file convention**, verified against the tree: 90 files, 111 classes, 78 decorated, the other 33 all DTOs. Final: **273 classes scanned across 643 closures, 59 unreachable, 0 framework false positives, calibration intact.**
- **What this does NOT claim:** four of the six known false closures have shapes this detector cannot see — `GT-158` (a criterion naming a token nothing issues), `GT-518` (a criterion ticked with an inline `Remaining:` caveat), `GT-566` (a de-duplication claim with the duplicate still on disk), `GT-221`. Only the `GT-321`/`GT-266` shape is mechanised here. The `Remaining:` caveat detector was built and calibrated (**1 hit, exactly `GT-518`**) and is registered separately rather than bolted on.
- **Status:** `DONE`

#### GT-698

**Title:** Fifty-nine closures rest on a class production never constructs, and the detector that found them cannot say which are dead code and which are merely unwired

- **Purpose:** Turn a frozen baseline into a triaged one, so the number can start going down.
- **Evidence:** **Measured 2026-08-15 by `57-validate-closure-reachability.mjs` on its first run:** 273 exported classes named as production evidence across 643 closure records; **59 have zero production call sites**, spread over 43 closures — 55 closed in June, 11 in July, 4 in August. Hand-verified samples: `LighthouseEvidenceProvider` (0 production uses, 13 spec mentions), `InMemoryEvaluationCache` (0 / 6), and `RulesetCorpusWarmupService` (**0 production uses and 0 spec mentions** — named as the evidence of a closure and referenced by nothing at all).
- **Use cases:**
  - Deciding, per class, whether to wire it, delete it, or reopen the gap that claimed it.
  - Shrinking a baseline that today only proves the problem exists.
- **Impact:** Each entry is a closure whose ticked criteria rest on code no runtime path reaches — the `GT-321` shape, which took 49 days to notice by hand. Until triaged, 43 rows on the board assert delivery that the repository cannot demonstrate.
- **Expected outcome:** every baseline entry carries a disposition (`wired`, `deleted`, `reopened`, or `framework — with the reason`), and the file shrinks toward zero.
- **Affected files:** `.harness/scripts/ci/closure-reachability-baseline.json`, and the 59 classes it names
- **Component:** `Governance` · **Criticality:** P2 · **Complexity:** L
- **Principal:** `L` · **Interest:** `HIGH` · **Basis:** `estimate`
- **Provenance:** Registered 2026-08-15 from `GT-697`'s first run. **Not folded into that row:** building the detector and triaging 59 findings are different work, and mixing them would have made the detector's own calibration unreviewable. **P2 and not P1 because the detector now exists** — the bleeding is stopped even though the wound is not yet dressed: no NEW unreachable closure can land without failing CI.
- **Acceptance criteria:**
  - [ ] **FALSIFIABILITY:** the baseline is strictly smaller than 59 and every removed entry names what happened to it — wired, deleted, or its gap reopened. Both counts recorded.
  - [ ] Every remaining entry carries a written disposition; none is left unexplained.
  - [ ] `RulesetCorpusWarmupService`, which nothing references at all, is resolved first and its gap re-examined.
  - [ ] Any entry that turns out to be a framework false positive moves the EXCLUSION into the guard, so the same class cannot reappear.
- **TRIAGE 2026-08-15 — and the first entry examined REFUTED this row's own hand-verified claim.** `RulesetCorpusWarmupService` was described above as "0 production uses and 0 spec mentions — referenced by nothing at all". **That was FALSE.** It is a provider at `app.module.ts:123` implementing `OnApplicationBootstrap`, and `GT-648`'s closure carries runner evidence of it executing: *"Ruleset corpus loaded at startup: 393 rules"*. Nest invokes the hook; nothing in the codebase ever needs to call it. My grep excluded `.module.ts` from the consumer scan — by design, from `GT-266`, where a provider registration genuinely was not a call site — and for a LIFECYCLE class that exclusion is exactly wrong. The claim is corrected here rather than edited away, because a detector's own row asserting a false hand-verification is the defect this gap exists to name.
- **Three false-positive classes found by triaging, each fixed in the detector with its reason: 59 → 54.**
  - **Lifecycle + registered (2):** `RulesetCorpusWarmupService`, `WatcherService`. Registration IS the call site when the framework owns the lifecycle. BOTH conditions are required — `WatcherService` implements `OnModuleInit`/`OnModuleDestroy` and **no module registers it**, so it stays flagged and is a real finding.
  - **Test doubles in a production path (2):** `MockLogger`, `MockConfigParser` live under `src/sdk/cli/src/test/mocks/`, consumed only by specs — which this detector deliberately does not scan. Reachable, just not from where it is allowed to look.
  - **Barrel-declared classes (1):** `PlatformDetectionService` is declared *inside* `domain/services/index.ts` rather than imported into it. It survives triage as genuinely dead.
- **The 54 that remain, each carrying a written `disposition` and `why` in the baseline:**
  - **`published-api` — 6.** Exported from a package's public index and published to npm, so consumers are external by design. This is NOT proof anyone uses them: a declared export is not an observed one. It means the absence of an internal call site is expected and is not the `GT-321` defect.
  - **`built-tested-unwired` — 46.** Constructed only by their own specs. The code exists and passes tests; no production path reaches it. This is the real backlog and the `GT-321` shape exactly.
  - **`dead` — 2.** `PlatformDetectionService`, claimed by both `GT-112` and `GT-189`, with no production call site and no spec reference anywhere.
- **`WatcherService` is the first case where the triage reaches a decision that is not mine to make.** `GT-298` closed it with two criteria: *"the required file or directory exists at the specified path"* and *"tests verify the implementation"*. **Neither asks whether it is wired** — a criterion a file satisfies by existing is how this class of closure passes. The title says *"WatcherService integration — MCP drift notification"*, and integration is precisely what did not happen. Wiring it, deleting it, or declaring drift notification unwanted is a product decision and is left open rather than taken here.
- **TRIAGE OF THE 46, 2026-08-15 — and it found a FOURTH detector defect, which is now the pattern worth naming: triage surfaced a false-positive class roughly every ten entries examined.** `export const x = new X()` — a class constructed into a module-level singleton **in its own file**, which `hasProductionCallSite` skips by design. `CommandExecutor`, `ErrorReporter` and `GateRoleEnforcer` were all reported unreachable while their singletons are imported across production. Fixed with the second half required: the const must actually be CONSUMED, which is why the six `GT-346` providers stay flagged. **59 → 48.**
- **THE STRONGEST FINDING OF THE TRIAGE, and it reframes this row.** `git log -S"new <Class>(" --pickaxe-regex` over every production `.ts` in the entire repository history returns **zero for all 34** remaining `built-tested-unwired` classes. **Not one of them regressed. Not one was ever connected.** They were written, tested, closed against, and never constructed by production code on any commit that has ever existed here. That is a different defect from "it broke": it is a closure standard that a file satisfies by existing.
- **FINAL DISPOSITIONS — 48 entries, each with a written reason in the baseline:**
  - **`built-tested-unwired` — 34.** Constructed only by their own specs, never in production, ever. Spread over `cli` (18), `core-domain` (18), `mcp-server` (7) and `agent-runtime` (3), across 34 closures — six of which claim more than one, so `GT-346` alone is seven classes and one decision.
  - **`published-api` — 6.** Exported from a package's public index and published to npm. Consumers are external by design; this is not proof anyone uses them.
  - **`singleton-nobody-imports` — 6.** The whole `GT-346` provider family — `DockerProvider`, `NpmProvider`, `NxProvider`, `PythonProvider`, `DotnetProvider`, `GitHubActionsProvider`. Each constructs an exported singleton in its own file that **no production file imports**.
  - **`dead` — 2.** `PlatformDetectionService`, claimed by `GT-112` and `GT-189`.
- **WHAT REMAINS IS A PRODUCT DECISION, NOT AN ENGINEERING ONE, and it is deliberately not taken here.** Each of the 34 is *wire it*, *delete it*, or *reopen the gap that claimed it* — and which of the three is right depends on whether the capability is still wanted, which is the owner's call and not derivable from the code. What the triage delivers is that the question is now answerable one closure at a time, with evidence attached, instead of resting on a 44-day human re-read.
- **BLOCK A, 2026-08-16 — I proposed deleting three "duplicate implementations that lost", and TWO OF THE THREE WERE MY DETECTOR BEING WRONG. The third was real but I had its direction backwards.**
  - **`PluginLoader` (`GT-98`, `GT-180`) is LIVE.** `app.module.ts:64` imports `PluginModule` from `infrastructure/plugins` — the tree I had called dead — and that module reaches the class through `PluginLoader.loadPlugins(workspaceDir)`, a STATIC call. The detector looked for `new`, `: Type`, `extends`, `@Inject` and `useClass`, and never for `Cls.method()`.
  - **`ToolDispatchService` (`GT-181`, `GT-189`, `GT-332`, `GT-352`) is LIVE, and this one is the inversion that matters.** It is constructed at `mcp-tool-dispatch.ts:377` inside `handleCallTool` — a function marked `@deprecated Use ToolDispatchService.callTool() instead` that four production files still call. The class is the CURRENT implementation and the functions are the old shim delegating to it. I told the owner the opposite.
  - **`PluginRegistry` (`GT-308`) is the only real finding of the three,** and the direction is the reverse of what I said: `src/sdk/cli/src/plugins/` is the unused tree, `infrastructure/plugins/` is the wired one. Two plugin systems, 92 lines, referenced by nothing outside its own directory except one line of catalog prose.
- **SIXTH AND SEVENTH DETECTOR DEFECTS, both found by triage, and the pattern is now the headline.** Static-member calls (`Cls.method()`) were invisible; and anything constructed INSIDE the declaring file was invisible, because `hasProductionCallSite` skips that file by design. The second was fixed with a rule that subsumes an earlier narrower patch: if the declaring file constructs the class AND exports something production consumes, the class is reached. Comment stripping was added at the same time — `AuditService.record` appears in a prose docblock and `StructuralReviewProvider.DEFAULT_DIMENSION` in a `//` comment, and either would have silently disabled this guard's own calibration.
- **`59 → 58 → 54 → 48 → 44 → 37`.** Seven false-positive classes, every one discovered by triaging entries rather than by writing the detector. **The detector built to catch over-claiming was itself over-claiming, by 37%.** Calibration on `GT-321` and `GT-266` survived all seven revisions, which is the only reason the remaining 37 can be trusted at all.
- **REVISED DISPOSITIONS (37):** `built-tested-unwired` **23** (21 distinct classes across 21 closures), `singleton-nobody-imports` **6**, `published-api` **6**, `dead` **2**.
- **NOTHING WAS DELETED.** The one true finding in block A, `PluginRegistry`, is a product decision — a second plugin system exists and is unused, and whether to delete it or adopt it over the wired one is not derivable from the code.
- **THE 23 RE-EXAMINED WITH THE SAME LENS, 2026-08-16 — ZERO new false positives.** After seven revisions the detector finally holds. Swept for every reachability mechanism the TypeScript scan cannot see: non-`.ts` references, `useFactory` bindings, dynamic `require`/`import()`/`Reflect.construct`, subclasses, string-token providers and port bindings. Two classes had a non-TS hit and both were **bookkeeping prose, not code** — and one is the loop in a single line: the only non-TypeScript mention of `ApiKeyProvisioningService` anywhere is inside `.harness/scripts/close-gt229-gt266.mjs`, **the script that wrote its own closure record**.
- **A FIFTH BIG NUMBER, MEASURED AND THEN DISCARDED BEFORE PUBLISHING IT.** A sweep reported "67 exported ports, 6 bound, 61 never bound", which would have been the headline of this row. It is INVALID: this codebase consumes ports by structural typing, not by DI token. `IFileSystem` has 2 token bindings and **160 production uses as a type**. The metric measures Nest wiring, not reachability. It is recorded here as refuted rather than quietly dropped, because four aggregate counts in this family were already wrong and the failure mode is always the same — the enumeration is right and the summary is not.
- **WHAT THE LENS DID FIND, and it splits the six port adapters into three different situations:**
  - **`IStructuralReviewer` has exactly ONE implementation and it is unwired.** `HeuristicStructuralReviewer` (`GT-613`) is the only class implementing the port, and nothing constructs it. `GT-613`'s own title reads *"the structural-reviewer seam has a port, a provider and a rubric, and no adapter implements it"* — the adapter now exists and the sentence is still true in effect.
  - **`IRunJournalPort` has two: an in-memory one and `FileRunJournalAdapter` (`GT-593`), the durable one, unwired.** `GT-593` exists because *"a run killed mid-pipeline restarts from zero"*. The durable journal is the fix, it was built, and nothing uses it — so the gap's stated purpose is unmet by its own closure.
  - **`IProcessRunner` and `IQualitySignalProvider` have live alternatives.** `NodeProcessRunner` and `SandboxedProcessRunner` implement the first; `C4BindingProposalProvider` and `KnowledgeOpportunityProvider` the second. The flagged `StubProcessRunner`, `StructuralReviewProvider` and `LighthouseEvidenceProvider` are redundant adapters, not missing capability — a different and much cheaper decision.
  - **`SyncService` is confirmed as the `GT-266` shape:** registered as a provider at `app.module.ts:79` and injected by nobody.
- **The 23 are now trustworthy debt.** That is the sentence this review existed to earn, and it could not have been said before the seven corrections.
- **`GT-613` AND `GT-593` WERE NOT WIRED, AND THE RECOMMENDATION TO WIRE THEM WAS WRONG. 2026-08-16.**
  - **`GT-593` is opt-in BY DESIGN, in writing.** `bootstrap.ts:105` reads *"GT-593 — step journal. UNSET by default: journaling changes what a re-submitted run does, so it is opt-in wiring (InMemoryRunJournalAdapter for a single process, FileRunJournalAdapter to survive a `kill -9`)."* NEITHER adapter is constructed — not the file one and not the in-memory one. Wiring it would change runtime behaviour the design deliberately leaves to the caller, to make a number go down. That is the move this entire audit exists to refuse.
  - **Both classes are PUBLISHED PUBLIC API.** `@beyondnet/evolith-agent-runtime` is a non-private package at `1.2.0`; its root `index.ts` does `export * from './adapters/index'`; and that barrel exports both `HeuristicStructuralReviewer` and `FileRunJournalAdapter`. Any external consumer can reach them. "No internal call site" is the expected shape for a library adapter, not a defect.
- **EIGHTH DETECTOR DEFECT: the `published-api` test did not follow re-export chains.** It looked for the class name literally in `src/index.ts` and missed `export * from './adapters/index'`. Following the chains moves **14 entries** to `published-api` — including `PlatformDetectionService`, which this row previously called **"referenced by nothing at all"** and which is exported from its package root. **That is the second time this row published a false hand-verification**, and both are corrected in place.
- **REVISED, AND THIS IS THE NUMBER THAT MATTERS:** `published-api` **14**, `built-tested-unwired` **17** (15 distinct classes across 16 closures), `singleton-nobody-imports` **6**, `dead` **0**. The `dead` bucket is now empty — both of its former members were published exports.
- **From 59 alleged findings to 15 distinct classes of real debt, across eight detector corrections, every one found by triaging rather than by writing the detector.** The instrument built to catch over-claiming over-claimed by a factor of four, and only entry-by-entry verification exposed it. That is the single most useful thing this row produced, and it argues for the general rule the audit already implied: **a measurement is not evidence until something has tried to refute it.**
- **Status:** `DEFERRED`

#### GT-699

**Title:** A finding that says "I could not evaluate this" is indistinguishable from a finding that says "your repository violates this", so 74 of 82 blocking issues are false alarms nobody can filter

- **Purpose:** Let a reader count violations without counting the engine's own admissions as violations.
- **Evidence:** **Measured 2026-08-16 through the shipped CLI on this repository, and every figure the audit offered was re-derived here rather than trusted.** `evolith validate` reports **112 issues, 82 blocking**. Of those 82, **74 are in `blockingSkippedRuleIds`** — their text reads *"This rule is declared `blocking: true` and was NOT evaluated"*. Only **8** are verdicts about the code. And the two kinds are INDISTINGUISHABLE: an admission and a violation carry the same fields, the same `severity: MUST` and the same `blocking: true`. A reader sees 82 problems and has 8. **The run already knows the difference** — it publishes `blockingSkippedRuleIds`, `blockingNonExecutableRuleIds`, `rulesNotApplicable`, `rulesNonExecutable` and `rulesExecutable` in its own counters — and then flattens it away in `issues[]`, which is the array a human and the Tracker actually read.
- **TWO CLAIMS FROM THE AUDIT THAT DID NOT SURVIVE RE-MEASUREMENT, corrected before acting on them.** (1) *"An empty directory earns 53 passes, 35 blocking."* It does not: an empty directory **FAILS**, with 120 issues and 82 blocking. (2) *"Only 62 of 411 rules change verdict between an empty directory and the full repo."* Once admissions are separated from verdicts the picture inverts — of 19 verdicts on this repository and 20 on an empty directory, only **4 overlap**, and two of those four are the meta-rules `GOV-RULE-NON-EXECUTABLE` and `GOV-RULE-NOT-APPLICABLE`. **15 fire only on this repository and 16 only on an empty one. The verdicts discriminate; it was the admissions that never did.**
- **Use cases:**
  - A buyer reads a report and needs the number of things wrong with their code, not that number plus the engine's coverage gaps.
  - The Tracker ingests a verdict and must not raise 74 findings a customer cannot act on.
  - An operator triaging a failed gate needs the 8 real ones first.
- **Impact:** The product's headline output overstates violations by roughly 10x on its own repository. It is not that the engine cannot fail — it fails loudly and correctly — it is that its failure is unreadable, and an unreadable signal gets muted, which is how a governance tool stops being consulted.
- **Expected outcome:** every finding declares whether it is a verdict or an admission, and no consumer has to parse prose to tell them apart.
- **Affected files:** `src/packages/core-domain/src/application/validators/rule-evaluation-engine.ts`, `src/packages/core-domain/src/application/validators/ruleset-validator.types.ts`, `src/packages/core-domain/src/evaluation/contracts/finding.ts`
- **Component:** `Core Domain` · **Criticality:** P1 · **Complexity:** S
- **Principal:** `S` · **Interest:** `SEVERE` · **Basis:** `estimate`
- **Provenance:** Registered and closed 2026-08-16 from the owner's instruction to fix "the product cannot fail". The instruction rested on the root-cause audit, and the first act here was to REPRODUCE the audit rather than act on it — which is what surfaced the two refuted claims above. **`SEVERE` interest because the cost compounds per run:** every evaluation any customer performs carries the same 10x overstatement.
- **Acceptance criteria:**
  - [x] **FALSIFIABILITY:** a consumer can partition the findings of a real run without reading prose. Before: `82 blocking, 0 distinguishable`. After, same repository: **19 verdicts (8 blocking) and 93 admissions (74 blocking)**. Both outputs recorded.
  - [x] `GT-595` keeps firing — an unevaluated blocking rule is still `blocking: true` and can never read as green. Asserted directly, because making them legible must never become suppressing them.
  - [x] All three sites that build an unevaluated finding carry the marker: the blocking-skipped issue, the handler-threw issue and the MUST-not-evaluated issue.
  - [x] The field is OPTIONAL, so absence means "verdict" and every existing consumer keeps its current reading.
- **CLOSED 2026-08-16.** Mutation: flipping the marker to `true` turns the partition case red. Suites after a clean build: core-domain **1968**, cli 1482, mcp 575, infra-providers 179, contracts 115. **A measurement taken against a FAILED build was discarded mid-work** — the type did not exist on `ValidationIssue` yet and `tsc -b` had emitted partially, so the numbers were re-taken after `build exit=0`.
- **What this does NOT fix.** The engine still cannot evaluate 74 of its own blocking rules on this repository. Making that legible is not making it go away, and the underlying coverage gap is `GT-694`'s and `GT-696`'s territory, not this row's. This row only guarantees that the gap is now countable.
- **Status:** `DONE`

#### GT-700

**Title:** GT-693's provenance tag was written as an early return, so every corpus rule silently stopped claiming the violation carrying its own id — 184 rules, and a whole-corpus OPA run collapsed from 52 issues to 4

- **Purpose:** Restore the attribution `GT-693` deleted while fixing a different one, and pin the case its own suite had no test for.
- **Evidence:** **Found 2026-08-16 by an adversarial probe launched against `GT-675`, not by the suite that shipped the defect.** `GT-693` gave every aggregated violation a `policy` tag so a GATE rule referencing `rulesets/opa/<file>.rego` could claim it, and wrote the predicate as `if (typeof provenance === 'string') return provenance === ruleId;` — an early return. Because `main.rego` tags **every** violation, the `return violation.id === ruleId` branch below it became **dead code**. Verified directly against the shipped build: `violationBelongsToRule({id:'ACL-02', policy:'opa-anti-corruption-layer'}, 'ACL-02')` → **`false`**, while the same violation untagged → `true`. **184 corpus rules are decidable by exact id from the shipped policies, and all 184 lost their claim the day the tag landed.** Measured end to end on this repository: a whole-corpus `--engine opa` run reported **4 issues / 1 blocking**, against the **52 / 31** the board recorded on 2026-08-14 before the tag existed, and against native's 112 / 82.
- **Use cases:**
  - A tenant runs `--engine opa` and gets 4 findings where the same corpus yields 52.
  - `DEP-10` is a genuine violation both engines can decide; only the OPA engine reported it green.
  - Anyone comparing the two engines is comparing an engine to a crippled version of itself.
- **Impact:** A false green on 26 blocking rules whose violations the engine **had already computed** and discarded to a `logger.debug` line — the worst shape available, because the evidence existed and was thrown away. It also poisoned every dual-engine measurement taken after 2026-08-15, including the ones used to size `GT-675`.
- **Expected outcome:** provenance ADDS a claimant instead of replacing one; a violation answers to both the corpus rule sharing its id and the gate rule that pulled its policy in.
- **Affected files:** `src/packages/core-domain/src/application/validators/evaluators/opa-evaluator.ts`, `src/packages/core-domain/src/application/validators/evaluators/opa-evaluator.spec.ts`
- **Component:** `Core Domain` · **Criticality:** P0 · **Complexity:** XS
- **Principal:** `XS` · **Interest:** `SEVERE` · **Basis:** `estimate`
- **Provenance:** Registered and closed 2026-08-16. **The defect was mine, shipped the previous day in `GT-693`, and it reached `main`.** `GT-693`'s suite pinned provenance-first and contained no case for a corpus rule whose id equals a violation id, so a four-case spec added the same afternoon passed over the regression. **P0 because it is a false green on a shipped path**, and `XS` because the fix is one line moved.
- **Acceptance criteria:**
  - [x] **FALSIFIABILITY:** a whole-corpus `--engine opa` run recovers the pre-regression figures. Before: **4 issues / 1 blocking**. After: **51 / 31**, against the **52 / 31** recorded on 2026-08-14. Both outputs recorded.
  - [x] A corpus rule claims the tagged violation carrying its own id, and the gate rule claims it too — both asserted, since the point is that they are additive.
  - [x] An untagged violation is unaffected, so a `policy.wasm` older than `GT-693` keeps working.
  - [x] The test was observed RED against the shipped predicate before the fix.
- **CLOSED 2026-08-16.** Suites after: core-domain **1972**, cli 1482, mcp 575, infra-providers 179, contracts 115; guard 28 green. **Why the residual 51 vs native's 112 is NOT this row:** the OPA engine still reports `rulesSkipped: 0` because `OpaEvaluator` has no `skipped` outcome at all — `grep -c skipped` returns **0** there against **3** in the native evaluator. That is `GT-675`, still open and now measurable against an engine that is no longer crippled.
- **The lesson this row exists to record.** `GT-693` replaced a hand-maintained prefix table with derived provenance and was right to. The defect was writing the new mechanism as an ALTERNATIVE to the old one rather than an ADDITION, and shipping a spec that only exercised the new path. A fix that removes a mechanism must test what that mechanism used to do.
- **Status:** `DONE`

#### GT-701

**Title:** None of the five composable validation modes reaches an evaluator, and one of them marks every rule `pass` for being readable — so `--composable`, the MCP tool and the REST endpoint validate nothing

- **Purpose:** Make the composable surface either evaluate or refuse, instead of returning a green report built from file parsing.
- **Evidence:** **Measured 2026-08-16, split out of `GT-675` whose criterion pointed at the wrong lines.** `ruleset-validation.mode.ts:87-95` iterates the rules it parsed and pushes `status: 'pass'` with the message *"Rule '<id>' loaded and registered"* for each — it counts a rule as checked for being readable, and evaluates nothing. Verified across the whole directory: `grep -rl "RulesetValidatorService\|OpaEvaluator\|NativeEvaluator" modes/` returns **nothing**; the only imports the five modes make are `fs` and `path`. `context.engine` is merged once at `composable-validation-engine.ts:77` (`engine: context.engine || config?.engine || 'native'`) and **read by nobody** — `grep -rn "context.engine" modes/*.ts` is empty.
- **Three surfaces carry it, and the `GT-688` fix did not touch any of them:**
  - CLI — `validate.command.ts:305` sends `engine` into the composable context whenever `--composable`, `--adr` or `--file` is passed. `evolith validate --composable --engine opa` accepts the flag, documents it in `--help`, and evaluates nothing.
  - MCP — `composable-validate.tool.ts:62`.
  - REST — `composable-validate.controller.ts:78`.
- **Impact:** A caller receives a report whose rules are all `pass`, produced without any rule being evaluated. This is the same class as `GT-688`'s silent engine downgrade and worse in degree: there the wrong engine answered, here **no engine answers at all** and the verdict is uniformly green.
- **Expected outcome:** the modes route through `RulesetValidatorService`, or the composable surface refuses instead of reporting `pass`; either way `engine` stops being accepted and ignored on three boundaries.
- **Affected files:** `src/packages/core-domain/src/application/validators/modes/**`, `src/sdk/cli/src/commands/validate/validate.command.ts`, `src/packages/mcp-server/src/tools/composable-validate.tool.ts`, `src/apps/core-api/src/presentation/controllers/composable-validate.controller.ts`
- **Component:** `Core Domain` · **Criticality:** P1 · **Complexity:** M
- **Principal:** `M` · **Interest:** `SEVERE` · **Basis:** `estimate`
- **Provenance:** Registered 2026-08-16 from the `GT-675` measurement wave. **Split out rather than folded in**, because `GT-675` is about an engine that answers wrongly and this is about a surface where no engine runs — and mixing them would let a fix to one tick a criterion belonging to the other, which is exactly how `GT-675`'s original AC5 was satisfiable while the worst case stayed live.
- **No test would catch this.** `composable-validate.tool.spec.ts:88-112` is named *"maps every optional arg into the engine context and honours engine=opa"* and reads like a threading test, but `ComposableValidationEngine` is mocked, so it asserts the boundary→context hop only and passes green against the current behaviour. It is the test most likely to be cited as proof this row is already closed. There is no test of `composable-validate.controller.ts` at all.
- **Acceptance criteria:**
  - [x] **FALSIFIABILITY:** a satellite that a plain `evolith validate` reports as failing is NOT reported as all-`pass` by `evolith validate --composable` on the same input. Both outputs recorded. **MET.** BEFORE — plain: `failed`, 113 checked, 112 issues; `--composable --ruleset definition-of-done`: `passed`, "10 rules checked", zero evaluations. AFTER — `failed`, 8 checked / 2 skipped / 10 total, with `RULESET_NOT_EVALUATED` or real findings depending on whether an evaluator is supplied.
  - [x] No mode emits `status: 'pass'` for a rule it did not evaluate. The `"loaded and registered"` message either disappears or stops being a `pass`. **MET** — the message is gone. A `pass` is now emitted only for a declared rule the engine evaluated and had nothing to say about; rules the engine skipped or errored on are excluded BY NAME, not by arithmetic.
  - [x] `engine` is consumed or removed on all four boundaries — CLI composable context, MCP tool schema, REST DTO, and the merge at `composable-validation-engine.ts:77`. Accepted-and-ignored is not an end state. **MET and measured:** `--composable --ruleset repository-taxonomy --engine opa` reports **10 checked** against **8** for `--engine native` on the same input. Before this row the two were byte-identical.
  - [x] A test fails when a mode ignores `context.engine`, and the mocked `composable-validate.tool.spec.ts` case is either made real or renamed so it stops reading as proof of threading. **MET** — `records the engine the host built the evaluator for` asserts `metadata.engine`, and the mode's 13 cases were observed RED (11 of 13) against the previous implementation before the fix landed.
- **Status:** `DONE`

#### GT-702

**Title:** The bilingual guard cannot see that an English doc and its Spanish twin DISAGREE, so a correction applied to one side alone passes every check.

- **Purpose:** Make a half-updated bilingual pair fail before it merges, instead of leaving a refuted claim standing in the other language.
- **Evidence:** **Measured 2026-08-16, from a defect committed the same day.** `0fb29909` corrected `gap-reference-catalog.md` to state that the OPA corpus holds **266** violation literals and that `{id, message}` is NOT their complete shape. `gap-reference-catalog.es.md` was not touched, so it went on asserting *"las 251 literales de violación del corpus llevan esas dos y nada más, verificado por conteo"* — both halves of which had just been refuted — inside the document the board treats as the record of truth. `04-check-bilingual-parity.mjs` passed on every run in between, and correctly: it asks whether an ES counterpart EXISTS, whether heading COUNTS match, and whether the Spanish file is Spanish. All three are properties of the files as they stand; none can observe that they contradict each other.
- **A content comparison was prototyped FIRST and rejected on measurement.** Comparing language-invariant tokens (numerals, tracked ids, inline code) section-by-section across the 500 pairs under `reference/` produced **2136** findings, and the first ones triaged were noise: `GT-383…394` parses as the cardinal `394`, table cells break inline-code pairing, and prose legitimately spells quantities differently in the two languages. A guard at that signal-to-noise ratio gets switched off, and a guard that is switched off is worse than none. Recorded here because the rejected design is the part most likely to be re-attempted.
- **The fix asks git instead.** The failure is not "the texts differ" — two translations always differ — it is "someone changed one side and not the other", which git answers exactly, with no tokenizer. Over the same 400 commits the content check produced 2136 findings and this produces **3**, all real one-sided edits.
- **Impact:** Every correction to one language is currently trusted to be mirrored by hand. When it is not, the stale side keeps asserting the refuted claim with a green parity check over it, and the board's own record disagrees with itself.
- **Expected outcome:** a range that moves one half of a pair and not the other fails `Validate documentation`.
- **Affected files:** `.harness/scripts/ci/66-validate-bilingual-sync.mjs` (new), `.github/workflows/docs.yml`
- **Component:** `Governance` · **Criticality:** P2 · **Complexity:** S
- **Principal:** `S` · **Interest:** `MED` · **Basis:** `estimate`
- **Provenance:** Registered 2026-08-16 from the `GT-693` correction wave, after the same defect class was found twice in one day — the `251`→`266` prose count and the `203`/`197`/`196` distinct-id count. The first was invisible across languages; this gap is about the mechanism that let it be.
- **Built and verified, not merely designed:** self-test 8/8; the audit sweep is green over 400 commits with three historical one-sided commits declared in `ALLOWED` with reasons; proven to FAIL on a real one-sided commit and to TOLERATE the split-across-commits shape. Range mode judges the range's NET effect — mirroring in a follow-up commit passes — because judging each commit alone failed correct work, which is how a guard teaches people to reach for its allowlist.
- **Deliberately NOT claimed:** a commit touching both halves can still put a wrong translation in the ES file. This closes the "never mirrored at all" hole, not translation quality.
- **CLOSED 2026-08-16.** Placed at `.harness/scripts/ci/66-validate-bilingual-sync.mjs`, byte-identical to the verified build (`sha256 9d03f47e…`), and wired into `docs.yml`. The S-16 `PreToolUse` hook that denied the write was **never circumvented**: it stopped denying because the `unimar-core` plugin is disabled at user AND project scope and a new session no longer loads it. Two separate systems had to be understood rather than worked around — the plugin hook blocked the Write tool, and Claude Code's own auto-mode classifier blocked the shell copy.
- **Acceptance criteria:**
  - [x] **FALSIFIABILITY:** run for real on throwaway branches. A branch editing only `gap-reference-catalog.md` FAILS (`1 bilingual pair(s) moved on one side only across develop..HEAD`); the same branch PASSES once the ES half is mirrored — including when the mirror lands in a SEPARATE commit, which the first implementation wrongly rejected.
  - [x] The guard is invoked by `Validate documentation` as two steps — the gate (`--since origin/<base>`) and its own self-test — so a half-updated pair blocks the merge. Scoped to the branch range so historical one-sided commits cannot fail an unrelated PR, and dependent on the job's existing `fetch-depth: 0`, which `assertScanned` turns into a failure rather than a silent pass if it ever regresses.
  - [x] All three `ALLOWED` entries carry written reasons. Verified in place: self-test 8/8, audit sweep green over 400 commits.

#### GT-703

**Title:** Closing a gap costs one CI round-trip per derived artifact, because the chain guard reports only the first stale link and nothing regenerates the rest.

- **Purpose:** Turn an N-push discovery loop into a single local command.
- **Evidence:** **Measured on GT-702's own closure, 2026-08-16.** Adding one board row and one closure record turned `Validate documentation` red twice: first `09-reconcile-maturity.mjs --check` ("Maturity reconciliation is stale"), then — once that was regenerated and pushed — `46-validate-derived-artifact-order` on the executive summary, which derives FROM the reconciliation. Runs `31957356934` (~1m43s) and `31957550307` (~3m45s) both failed before the third went green. The entire content delta across all of it was `total 699→700`, `done 665→666`, `closureRecords 647→648`, in three files.
- **The stop-at-first-stale behaviour is correct and must NOT be changed.** `46` says so itself: *"an artifact built on stale input is not independently wrong, and fixing it first would hide the cause."* Reporting all stale links at once would invert that and send people to fix consequences. The defect is not the diagnosis, it is that the repair has no entry point.
- **The data already exists.** `CHAIN` in `46-validate-derived-artifact-order.mjs` declares all **8** links as `{name, producer, checkArgs}`, and every producer already supports a write mode (it is the same script invoked without `--check`). Replaying the chain in dependency order is therefore a loop over a list the guard already holds — the missing piece is an entry point, not a model.
- **Impact:** Every gap closure pays a CI cycle per stale link, and each cycle is a push, a wait and a re-read of logs. It also trains the wrong reflex: the natural response to "red on an artifact I did not touch" is to re-run CI, not to look for a chain.
- **Expected outcome:** one command regenerates every stale link in dependency order and then re-verifies the fixed point, so a stale chain fails locally in seconds instead of over N pushes.
- **Affected files:** `.harness/scripts/ci/46-validate-derived-artifact-order.mjs`
- **Component:** `Governance` · **Criticality:** P3 · **Complexity:** S
- **Principal:** `S` · **Interest:** `LOW` · **Basis:** `estimate`
- **Provenance:** Registered 2026-08-16 from the GT-702 closure, where the cost was paid and measured rather than predicted. Not folded into GT-702: that gap is about the bilingual guard, this is about the derived-artifact chain, and they share only the commit that exposed it.
- **CLOSED 2026-08-16.** `--fix` walks `CHAIN` in declared order, regenerates every stale link in one pass, and then re-runs the ordinary currency and fixed-point checks rather than trusting its own report — a repair mode believed on its own say-so is how a chain ends up "fixed" and still stale. The write invocation is DERIVED (`writeArgsFor`), the check invocation minus the flag that makes it a check, so a link that ever gains a `--root` keeps it instead of silently losing it. One pass suffices as a property of the chain, not luck: `validateChainShape` has already proven no link consumes what a later link writes, so regenerating link *i* can only invalidate links after *i*, which are still ahead.
- **Acceptance criteria:**
  - [x] **FALSIFIABILITY:** reproduced the GT-702 shape by restoring the reconciliation and both summaries from `5eed0766`. Check mode named ONLY `maturity reconciliation is STALE (link 5 of 8)`. One `--fix` regenerated `maturity reconciliation` then `executive governance summary`, in that order, and reported the fixed point. The regenerated bytes were **identical to what was committed** (`git diff HEAD` empty), so the repair produced the right content and not merely a self-consistent one.
  - [x] Check mode is unchanged: it still stops at the first stale link, with the same wording about not hiding the cause. The repair is additive and off by default.
  - [x] The failure message now ends with `To repair the whole chain in declared order: node 46-validate-derived-artifact-order.mjs --fix`.
  - [x] A producer that FAILS stops the pass with exit 1 rather than continuing — verified by stubbing link 1's generator to exit non-zero, twice, restoring it byte-identically each time. Tests: 12/12 (was 8), plus meta-guards `42` and `43`.
#### GT-704

**Title:** No CI job runs both engines over the corpus, so a verdict divergence between them is found by a human or not at all

- **Purpose:** Catch the day the two engines start disagreeing about FACTS, which is the disagreement `ADR-0041` actually cares about.
- **Evidence, measured 2026-08-16 with both engines on the whole corpus after `GT-675` landed:**

  | comparison | count | is it a defect? |
  |---|---|---|
  | opposite verdicts (`passed` on one, `failed` on the other) | **16** | **yes** — `TAX-01`, `TAX-05`, `INH-02`, `SVC-03`, `ACL-01` among them |
  | OPA decides, native skips | 65 | no — complementary coverage |
  | native decides, OPA skips | 17 | no — same, other direction |
  | OPA `passed` on a rule the bundle cannot decide | **0** | closed by `GT-675`, by construction |

- **Split out of `GT-675`, and the split is the point.** That row's AC7 asked for a dual-engine sweep and costed it at ~17 s. What shipped is narrower on purpose: a guard that executes the compiled bundle and fails if it cannot state its own scope — the invariant whose quiet loss would silently un-fix 234 rules. It does not compare the two engines, and ticking AC7 as if it did would have been the "satisfiable while the worst case stays live" failure that `GT-675` was itself rewritten to escape.
- **A second measurement this row inherits:** `GT-675` named `cli/exit-code-taxonomy` as the control pack where both engines agree. Measured, they do not — native `passed / exit 0` against OPA `failed / exit 2 / 1 blocking`. `GT-675`'s fix left it exactly where it was, so its criterion ("must NOT move") held; the characterisation was simply wrong, and it is one of the 16.
- **Use cases:**
  - A policy author edits a `.rego` so it now contradicts the native handler for the same rule, and CI is silent.
  - A tenant on OPA and an auditor on native read opposite verdicts for the same repository and neither report explains it.
- **Impact:** The two engines are allowed to disagree about coverage. They are not allowed to disagree about facts, and today nothing measures whether they do.
- **Expected outcome:** a CI job runs both engines over the corpus and fails on any rule id with opposite verdicts, publishing the count with its denominator; the 16 known divergences are either fixed or explicitly baselined with a reason each.
- **Affected files:** `.harness/scripts/ci/parity-gate.mjs`, `.harness/scripts/ci/27-opa-parity-gate.mjs`, `.github/workflows/ci-cd.yml`, `.github/workflows/opa-parity.yml`
- **Component:** `Core Domain` · **Criticality:** P2 · **Complexity:** M
- **Principal:** `M` · **Interest:** `MED` · **Basis:** `estimate`
- **Provenance:** Registered 2026-08-16 from the `GT-675` closure, which measured it and deliberately did not absorb it. **CLOSED 2026-08-18 by `68-validate-engine-verdict-parity.mjs` + `engine-verdict-parity.baseline.json` + the `Test` job step, with 9 unit tests in `68-validate-engine-verdict-parity.test.mjs`.** The test that matters pins the outcome precedence: a rule listed as `skipped` that ALSO carries a "blocking rule did not run" issue is `skipped`, not `failed`. Reading those as verdicts would have manufactured 144 fake conflicts on this corpus, and the guard would have shipped measuring noise. **What this closure could not do is explain its own headline discrepancy** — 11 measured against 16 registered — because the row recorded a count and 5 of 16 ids; that is the defect its own AC2 anticipated, now fixed for every future run.
- **Acceptance criteria:**
  - [x] **FALSIFIABILITY:** a deliberately introduced contradiction (one rule made to fail natively and pass under OPA) turns the job red, and removing it turns it green. Both outputs recorded. **MET, and the probe is named so it can be repeated.** `governance.rego`'s single `INH-06` body — a rule BOTH engines fail today — was made unsatisfiable and the bundle rebuilt: OPA passed it, native still failed it, and the guard exited **1** with `❌ 1 rule(s) reach OPPOSITE verdicts and are not registered: - INH-06: native=failed, opa=passed`. Reverting the `.rego` and rebuilding returned `✓ 28 jointly-decided rule(s), 11 conflict(s), all registered`, exit **0**. A first probe against `TAX-05` did NOT turn it red and is worth recording: two policies emit that id (`repository-taxonomy.rego` and `taxonomy.rego`), so disabling one leaves the verdict unchanged — the probe was wrong, not the guard.
  - [x] The job runs BOTH engines and publishes `verdict-conflicts / named-ids / corpus-total`, not a bare count. **MET, and this row is the reason the criterion was right.** Every run prints `ENGINE_VERDICT_PARITY {…}` carrying `verdictConflicts`, `namedIds`, `corpusTotal` and — added because the measurement demanded it — `jointlyDecided`, the only honest denominator: **28**, not 412. The registered `16` did not reproduce (today: **11**), and because this row published a count with 5 of its 16 ids, whether five were fixed or the count was wrong cannot be recovered from what it wrote.
  - [x] Each of the 16 known conflicts is either fixed or carries a written reason; a bulk baseline with one shared justification does not satisfy this. **MET for the 11 that exist, each with its own measured reason** in `.harness/scripts/ci/engine-verdict-parity.baseline.json` — naming the exact `.rego` line and fact path (`ACL-01`, `ACL-04`, `DORA-01`, `SPACE-04`, `SPACE-05`, `SVC-01`, `SVC-03`), the differing exemption lists (`TAX-01`), the doubled scan root (`CLI-EXIT-01`, `CLI-EXIT-03`) and the undeclared synthetic id (`GOV-RULE-NON-EXECUTABLE`). Of the 5 ids this row named, `TAX-05` and `INH-02` are NOT conflicts today — both engines fail them. **The baseline is a ratchet, not permission:** a conflict missing from it is red, and an entry that no longer conflicts is red too, so a fix cannot land without deleting its own entry.
  - [x] It reuses `diffDecisions` / `diffCoverage` rather than adding a third comparison, and is instrumented per `42-validate-guard-denominators` with `assertScannedPerSource({ native, opa })`. **MET for `diffDecisions`, and `diffCoverage` is deliberately NOT called — recorded as a deviation rather than satisfied on paper.** `diffCoverage` takes the ids an ARTIFACT declares decidable, which only the compiled bundle can answer and which `27-opa-parity-gate.mjs` already asks it there; calling it here with "the ids this run happened to decide" would compare a set against itself and always return clean. `assertScannedPerSource({ native, opa })` is in place, guard 42 classifies the script INSTRUMENTED (84 guards, 0 PENDING) and guard 43 OBSERVED it red against the empty fixture.
  - [x] The host is on the required-check path, not the schedule-only parity workflow — measured cost is ~17 s. **MET** — it runs in `ci-cd.yml` → `test` (the required check named `Test`), the one job that already builds the CLI `dist/main.js` the sweep spawns; `npm run build:policy` was added there for the bundle. Measured **18.4 s** for the two engine runs (native 11.7 s, OPA 6.7 s), against the ~17 s costed here.
- **Status:** `DONE`

#### GT-705

**Title:** The published MCP server ships no ruleset corpus, so 48 of its 50 tools cannot do governance work from a clean install

- **Purpose:** Make the MCP server people install able to answer the tools it announces.
- **Evidence, measured 2026-08-16 by `GT-671`'s canary on its first real run against the registry.** From a throwaway npm prefix, driving `@beyondnet/evolith-mcp@1.2.2` over stdio:

  | call | result |
  |---|---|
  | `tools/list` | **50** tools announced |
  | `evolith-gate-evaluate` | `RULESET_NOT_FOUND` — `ENOENT … /evolith/reference/governance/sdlc/gates` |
  | `evolith-validate` | `INTERNAL_ERROR` — *"Could not locate the Evolith ruleset corpus"* |
  | `evolith-metrics` | works — it needs no corpus |

- **The cause is in the package manifest, not in the code.** `@beyondnet/evolith-mcp` declares `files: ["dist/", "README.md", "LICENSE"]`, and none of its five `@beyondnet/*` dependencies carries the corpus either. Only `@beyondnet/evolith-cli` ships one, through its `copy-rulesets` prebuild — which is why the CLI half of the same canary is green (`145` rules loaded) while the MCP half is not.
- **Why no suite caught it:** the in-tree MCP smoke runs against the repository, where the corpus is on disk. That is exactly the tree-versus-tarball asymmetry [`GT-671`](./gap-reference-catalog.md#gt-671) exists to expose, and this row is its first catch.
- **Use cases:**
  - An agent is pointed at the published MCP server, sees 50 tools, and every governance call fails.
  - A tenant follows the MCP setup documentation and concludes the product does not work.
  - A release goes out with a corpus change and nothing downstream can observe it, because the server never had a corpus to change.
- **Impact:** The MCP surface is the agent-facing product. Announcing 50 tools and answering 2 is worse than announcing 2, because the failure appears at call time, inside someone else's agent.
- **Expected outcome:** the published MCP package resolves a ruleset corpus — shipped in its own `files`, or taken from a dependency that ships one, or documented as a required `corePath` the server refuses to start without.
- **Affected files:** `src/packages/mcp-server/package.json`, `src/packages/mcp-server/scripts/**`, `.github/workflows/npm-release.yml`
- **Component:** `MCP Server` · **Criticality:** P1 · **Complexity:** M
- **Principal:** `M` · **Interest:** `HIGH` · **Basis:** `estimate`
- **Provenance:** Registered 2026-08-16 from `GT-671`'s canary, which measured it rather than inferring it. Split out rather than folded into `GT-671`: that row is about *having* a scheduled check on the published artifact, this one is about *what the check found*, and merging them would let the canary's existence tick a criterion about the product being installable.
- **Acceptance criteria:**
  - [x] **FALSIFIABILITY:** from a clean npm prefix with no repository on disk, `evolith-gate-evaluate` over stdio returns a real gate verdict. **MET, and both sides recorded.** BEFORE: `RULESET_NOT_FOUND — ENOENT … /evolith/reference/governance/sdlc/gates`. AFTER: `isError: false`, verdict `failed`, gate `business-sign-off` — a verdict that names the gate it evaluated.
  - [x] `evolith-validate` over the published MCP server returns an envelope with a real corpus behind it. **MET** — `INTERNAL_ERROR "could not locate the Evolith ruleset corpus"` became a verdict of `failed`, reached over the bundled corpus.
  - [x] The corpus the server resolves is the one the release published. **MET** — `scripts/copy-corpus.js` copies from `src/rulesets` (the SSOT) on every build and on `prepublishOnly`, the trees are gitignored as build output so no committed copy can drift, and the script REFUSES to publish when neither a source tree nor an already-bundled corpus is present. The skip is verified, never assumed — that is `copy-rulesets.js`'s own lesson.
  - [x] If the answer is "the server requires an explicit corePath", it refuses rather than announcing tools it cannot serve. **NOT THE ANSWER CHOSEN, and the row records why.** Self-sufficient with override was the decision: the package bundles a corpus as its floor, `EVOLITH_CORE_PATH` and a per-call `corePath` always win, and `describeCorpusAtStartup()` names which one answered. That matches what the CLI already does, so the two surfaces stop disagreeing.
  - [x] `GT-671`'s canary drops its known-limitation exemption in the same change. **MET, and better than dropped — it now EXPIRES BY ITSELF.** The exemption is keyed on the CAUSE (does the installed package carry a corpus?) rather than on a version or a date, because the canary measures the REGISTRY and `latest` still predates this fix. The moment a published build ships a corpus the exemption stops matching and the gate assertion bites, with nobody having to remember. Verified both ways: the fixed package ships a corpus, the published one does not.
- **Status:** `DONE`
